Introduction

Transducers are devices that transform one type of signal into another. Sensors are transducers that take a physical phenomenon and convert it into another form of energy that can be read and acted upon. This project is the development of a membrane potentiometer, a transducer that converts the position of a touch along a linear surface into a variable resistance. That resistance forms a voltage divider that the analog pin of a microcontroller can read.

Electrically, the device is not much different from a regular potentiometer. A potentiometer has 3 pins. Two of them have a fixed resistance between them. The third is connected to a wiper that, through the turn of a knob or the movement of a slider, picks the point along that resistance where it makes contact. This varies the resistance between the wiper pin and each of the 2 fixed pins.

Membrane potentiometers work through the interaction of conductive and resistive layers separated by an insulating spacer. Unlike a regular potentiometer, the variable pin is not always in contact with the resistive element. Only when pressure is applied does the membrane deform, letting the conductive layer touch the resistive material.

Motive

Membrane potentiometers have many real-world applications. When the principle is applied in 2 dimensions, it forms a resistive touch screen, still widely used in ATMs and industrial HMIs. My immediate reason for building this device was that I wanted a ribbon controller, an input device used by synthesizers to continuously control a tone’s pitch, similar to the string of a fretless instrument. I found that both ribbon controllers and standalone membrane potentiometers were too expensive for my budget, so I decided to design custom membrane potentiometers that I could incorporate into future musical projects.

Design and construction

The build started from a copper-laminated plate as the base. A dedicated CNC machine in my university’s maker workshop etched 3 main pads into it. The 2 smaller pads at either end are the voltage input and ground pins, and the central pad is the common output pin. On top sits a thin acetate layer that separates the resistive membrane from the output pad, with an opening that lets the two touch whenever pressure is applied.

The resistive membrane is a sheet of Velostat, a polymer impregnated with carbon particles. That makes it conductive, but with a notable resistance. Both ends of the membrane are in constant contact with the edge pads. Velostat’s flexibility makes it a good fit for the “membrane”. It does shed carbon particles when exposed to water or the elements, and it leaves fingers black after direct contact, so a protective acetate film goes on top. All plastic films were cut with a laser cutter and fastened to the PCB with M3 bolts.

Electrical characteristics

At rest there is no contact between the membrane and the output pin, so this design doubles as a switch. It also means that when the device is wired to a microcontroller as an analog input, the analog value floats whenever the membrane isn’t pressed, which ruins measurements. I recommend placing a fixed resistance between the output pin and ground to pull the signal down when the membrane isn’t touched. This fixes the floating pin, but the output signal is no longer directly linear with the touched position.

The complete model is the circuit below. R1 is the dynamic resistance, the part of the membrane that can make contact with the output pad. R2 is the pulldown resistance. R3 and R4 are the membrane resistances between the ends of the dynamic portion and the end contacts.

f is the analog input signal generated by this arrangement (a value between 0 and 1, as a fraction of Vin). p is the touched position across the dynamic range of the membrane (also between 0 and 1), measured here from the ground end.

f(p)=R2(R3+pR1)(R4+(1−p)R1)(R2+R3+pR1)+R2(R3+pR1)

This formula may be too complex to calculate continuously on a microcontroller. Once the potentiometer is built and the pulldown resistance is chosen, I recommend dividing the position domain into 2 or 3 regions where the output is assumed to be linear.

Conclusions

Though the initial prototype was rather crude, I was satisfied with the results, and with this membrane potentiometer design. It is easy to scale and to integrate into projects that already use PCBs in their construction. The only hard limitation is that Velostat is sold in square sheets with a side length of 25 cm, so any potentiometer made from it has to be smaller than that.

I have used this technology in further projects, specifically related to the original motive: the development of dedicated ribbon controller synthesizers.
